item.title: JosieVerse Enterprise (JVE): Foundational Charter and Baseline Architecture of MultiDimensional Cognition (MDC), Creative Intelligence (CI), and Dimensional Relational Intelligence (DRI)
item.description:
[预印本] Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
ABSTRACT Contemporary conversation around artificial intelligence is caught between two incomplete extremes. At one end sits unstructured, transactional prompting, which frequently flattens an author's natural voice. At the other end sits corporate information-technology compliance, which treats artificial intelligence purely as passive software or enterprise risk to be audited. Neither approach addresses what happens when an independent thinker and advanced artificial intelligence systems work together as partners across sustained intellectual and artistic creation. JosieVerse Enterprise (JVE) establishes a third path. Founded by poet, researcher, and systems architect Josie O. Magee Bélanger, JVE is a creative, literary, and research enterprise anchored in the foundational field of MultiDimensional Cognition (MDC) and its innate parallel-processing construct, MultiDimensional Intelligence (MDI). Sitting beneath and powered by MDC are the two operational spheres of JVE's ten-domain architecture: 1. Creative Intelligence (CI): The artistic and structural sphere of JVE, comprising four domains: Dimensional Perspective Writing (DPW), Dimensional Perspective Systems (DPS), Creative Systems Architecture (CSA), and Dimensional Perspective AI (DPAi). 2. Dimensional Relational Intelligence (DRI): The relational and governance sphere of JVE, comprising six domains: Governance and Safety Architecture (GOV), H+AI Relational Architecture (HAI), Multi-Model Collaboration Architecture (MMCA), Dimensional Communication Systems (DCS), Dimensional Communication Engineering (DCE), and Nervous-System-Aware Design (NSAD). Together, these six domains define how people and AI collaborators communicate, pace complex work, maintain role boundaries, and preserve personal sovereignty across sustained collaboration. Unlike conceptual frameworks that begin and end as abstract theory, JosieVerse Enterprise is anchored in completed literary art, including the inaugural poetry duology Beneath the Gathered Shade: Poems of Lineage, Seasons, and Survival (Volume I) and The Forever Drifting Poem: And Other Works of Dimensional Poetic Art (Volume II). This Foundational Charter establishes priority of conception and public baseline definitions across the entire architecture, followed by ten adoptable principles for human+AI practice and a concise Quick-Reference Glossary for readers. ACM CCS: H.1.2 (User/Machine Systems: Human Factors); H.5.3 (Group and Organization Interfaces / Collaborative Computing); I.2.0 (Artificial Intelligence: Philosophical Foundations); J.5 (Arts and Humanities: Literature).

item.title: Generative AI and Meaning-Making in Media and Communication: A Systematic Review of Semiotic Perspectives (2021–2026)
item.description:
Information
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping media and communication, yet research on its semiotic role in meaning-making remains theoretically and methodologically fragmented. This systematic review examines semiotic frameworks, technological modalities, communication contexts, and human–AI agency in research published from 2021 to 26 August 2026. Scopus and Web of Science searches identified 376 records; the final included corpus comprises 128 studies. The synthesis distinguishes between modality-specific concerns: studies of large language models primarily examine interaction and dialogue, whereas text-to-image studies emphasize representation and synthetic imagery. The RAW agency data contained four cases coded as predominantly AI-led, but these classifications changed following a documented text-consistency review, showing that the agency pattern is sensitive to coding decisions. We derive four provisional configurations: instrumental human anchoring, mediated distributed semiosis, co-creative/agentive participation, and contested or unresolved computational semiosis. The studies also reveal interconnected methodological, conceptual, cultural, technological, and governance gaps. These findings suggest that participation in sign production and mediation should be distinguished from claims of autonomous intentional agency; they do not establish whether generative systems possess intentional understanding.

item.title: Development of participatory intervention to improve safety and enjoyment in sports events based on Participatory Action-Oriented Training
item.description:
Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
Introduction Sports events are leisure activities that contribute to public well-being. To maximize their benefits, large-scale improvements and the continuous accumulation of small, low-cost, and immediately actionable improvements are needed. However, systematic approaches for the improvement of safety and enjoyment in sports events remain limited. Hence, this study developed and evaluated the Sports Event Improvement for Safe, Move, Info, Link, and Environment (SMILE) program based on Participatory Action-Oriented Training (PAOT). Methods The SMILE program was developed using a research and development framework and evaluated through field research and questionnaire. Field research covered professional football, basketball, and rugby games in Japan. The program involved 294 participants in Day 1 fieldwork and 243 in Day 2 workshops. Output evaluation assessed good practices, improvement proposals based on the program design principle of balancing safety and enjoyment, club feedback, and participant satisfaction. Outcome evaluation examined pre–post changes in engagement with sports clubs, spectating, supporting, and participating in sports, and PAOT. Results Participants collected 2,951 photographs of good practices and proposed 174 improvements. Output evaluation demonstrated high participant satisfaction and positive club feedback. Outcome evaluation showed significant pre–post increases in engagement with sports and PAOT. A 30-item action checklist based on photographs was developed to support the program. Discussion The SMILE program was developed as a participatory approach to the sustained improvement of safety and enjoyment in sports events. It promotes the refinement and sharing of good practices, the accumulation of small, low-cost, and immediately actionable improvements, and value co-creation among stakeholders.

item.title: A conceptual co-design framework for structuring bankable climate interventions: design and illustrative instantiation
item.description:
Frontiers in Sustainable Cities
Urban and regional authorities across Europe must design climate-resilient interventions under constrained budgets, while coordinating more closely with private investors and insurance companies. Participatory governance, multi-criteria decision analysis and climate-investment planning are rarely combined in a single, transparent workflow. This is mainly because cities lack conceptual frameworks linking these elements across policy, technical design and finance. Here we report how the Horizon Europe BLOSSOM project used a design science research methodology in which an ArchiMate-based enterprise-architecture framework, structured around the analytic hierarchy process, developed the Co-design Framework for Bankable Climate Interventions (CFBCI), proposed as a reference architecture for participatory co-design of climate-resilient interventions. CFBCI is illustrated through a single instantiation in the River Cole urban-reforestation intervention in Birmingham, United Kingdom, one of seven BLOSSOM pilot sites across Europe; this instantiation demonstrates the framework’s structure and is not presented as a validated case. Representational completeness was examined through the Bunge–Wand–Weber ontological model and a co-creation session with BLOSSOM stakeholders. This formative evaluation, rather than a test of bankability or decision effectiveness, revealed three incompleteness gaps, one excess element, two redundancies and two overload issues, alongside general stakeholder interest and three refinements arising from the co-creation session: explicit legislative elements, flexible facilitator/expert roles for resource-constrained municipalities, and a simplified implementation guide. Together, these findings offer a conceptual reference architecture for structuring co-created climate solutions, providing a basis for future empirical validation and comparative research on urban sustainability transitions.

item.title: Psychological mechanisms of perceived technological dependence on generative artificial intelligence tools: perceived knowledge, trust, anxiety, and self-efficacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI tools are increasingly used in design education, yet the relationship between students’ perceptions of these tools and their reported reliance on them remains unclear. This study analyzed cross-sectional survey responses from 526 undergraduate students in design-related disciplines using partial least squares structural equation modeling. In the specified model, perceived reliability, perceived usefulness, and perceived intelligence were positively associated with perceived AIGC knowledge, whereas perceived ease of use was not significantly associated with it. Perceived AIGC knowledge was positively associated with trust, self-efficacy, and usage intention and negatively associated with AIGC-related anxiety. Trust, AIGC-related anxiety, and self-efficacy each showed a significant indirect effect in the modeled relationship between perceived AIGC knowledge and usage intention. Usage intention was strongly associated with perceived technological dependence. These findings are consistent with the proposed framework, but the cross-sectional data do not establish the temporal sequence of the constructs or show that reported dependence reflects harmful overuse. The study extends technology acceptance research by examining perceived reliance in AIGC-supported creative work.

item.title: Co-creating the EndoWatch - a smart wearable device for the management of hypothalamic dysfunction in pediatric brain tumor survivors: a pilot study
item.description:
Frontiers in Endocrinology
Introduction Hypothalamic dysfunction (HD) after treatment for a pediatric (supra)sellar tumor severely affects quality of life of patients, as well as their parents and families. Patients may develop signs of fatigue as a result of persistent disturbances in thermoregulation, sleep-wake rhythm, or hormonal insufficiencies. The management of HD requires around-the-clock care by the parent or caregiver. To support patients with HD and their parents/caregivers, we co-created a smart wearable device for continuous monitoring (EndoWatch) to detect early signs of hypothalamic dysregulation. We aimed to evaluate adherence to and user experiences of the first EndoWatch design. Methods In co-creation with clinicians, patient representatives, and design researchers and engineers, an existing smart device (wearable sensor and mobile application (app)) was adapted to a first design tailored for this purpose. In a prospective, observational study, 10 pediatric brain tumor survivors with HD (8 children; 2 adults) tested the first design of the device for 14 days. The primary outcome was adherence to wearing the EndoWatch. Secondary outcomes included usability, learnability, and desirability (through questionnaires), and barriers and facilitators (through semi-structured interviews). Results Ten patients participated (8 children, mean age 10.8 (SD 3.5); 2 adults, aged 18.9 and 31.0 years). Median overall adherence was 99.4% (IQR 22.8); two patients discontinued early due to wristband-related discomfort. Key facilitators were ease of use of the device and reliable technical performance. Main barriers included the absence of a separate caregiver app and limitations of the patient diary. These findings informed design modifications for future improvements of the device. Discussion The concept of the first EndoWatch design was considered acceptable and usable by patients with HD and their caregivers. This study identified key barriers and the modifications required for improvement, which were incorporated into a second EndoWatch design, to be evaluated in a larger prospective study.

item.title: Whitford, T. & Nyilasy, G. (2026, July 6–9). The critical GenAI debates facing business schools: Evidence from embedded classroom practice. [Poster Session], HERDSA Annual Conference, Singapore
item.description:
[预印本] University of Melbourne data repository
Our aim was to understand what happens when generative AI is deliberately embedded into postgraduate business education, rather than treated as an add-on, a threat, or a shortcut. Across Semester 1, 2025, we worked across two master’s subjects, co-designed with staff, founders and students, and used weekly studio-style workshops to examine how students actually used AI in entrepreneurial and business learning.The background is familiar to most of us now. GenAI can draft pitch decks, simulate investor meetings, produce market scans, and generate business ideas in seconds. So the question is no longer whether GenAI belongs in the classroom. It already does. The more important question is: what does it change about learning, judgement, creativity, evidence, and assessment?What we found was encouraging, but also complex. Students became more confident and capable with AI over the semester. Confidence rose from 6.38 to 7.46, and motivation also increased significantly. Students told us AI helped most with speed, brainstorming, structure, and getting unstuck. But they were also very clear about its limits. They worried about accuracy, generic outputs, overconfidence, and what some described as cognitive offloading, where AI becomes a reassurance machine rather than a thinking partner.The centre of the poster turns those findings into five debates: automation versus augmentation, efficiency versus ethics, levelling versus inequality, disciplinary boundaries versus interdisciplinarity, and simulation versus reflection. Each debate links a theoretical concern to a practical teaching response. For example, if AI accelerates thinking but risks generic work, then we need an “AI-starter, human-finisher” model. If AI makes work faster but students over-rely on it, then we need verification routines, such as the two-check rule. If AI can democratise learning but premium access creates inequity, then prompt libraries, shared tools, and studio-based peer learning become design questions, not optional extras.The contribution here is not simply that AI can be useful. We already know that. The contribution is a framework for educators: use AI to open possibilities, but use evidence, ethics, disciplinary judgement, and reflection to close decisions.Looking forward, the exciting direction is curriculum design. We need assessments that reward process, not just polished outputs. We need AI-free sprints to keep unaided judgement sharp. We need students comparing AI-only, human-only, and hybrid work. And at faculty level, we need shared AI literacy, clear guardrails, and equitable access.So the conclusion is simple: GenAI can be the starter motor, but educators and students still need to drive the vehicle. Taught deliberately, graduates can become both AI-literate and critically human.

item.title: Mapping The Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Group Creative Processes: A Scoping Review
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is finding its way into creative work at a growing pace, yet its specific role within collaborative creative processes, those involving multiple people working together, remains poorly understood and fragmented across the literature. This scoping review maps the empirical research on integrating GenAI into group creative processes, outlining creative domains, tasks, AI tools, AI roles, stages of integration, and reported outcomes. Following PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidance, a systematic search was conducted across Scopus, Web of Science, and PsycINFO. Empirical peer-reviewed studies were included when they involved at least two human participants engaged in a collaborative creative process supported by GenAI. Thirty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria. The majority were conducted in educational and design contexts, with brainstorming, content creation, and design development emerging as the most frequent task types. GenAI was most often integrated as a co-creative partner, typically during the ideation stage or across multiple phases of the creative process. Reported benefits included enhanced ideation, greater efficiency, improved engagement, and stronger collaboration quality, while the main tensions revolved around over-reliance on AI, cognitive offloading, homogenization of ideas, and unresolved questions of authorship and agency. Taken together, the findings suggest that GenAI is becoming an active component of hybrid human–AI creative systems, but whether its benefits are realized depends heavily on how collaborative workflows are designed to preserve human agency, support critical reflection, and maintain diversity of perspectives.

item.title: Creating Indigenous sovereign virtual spaces : accountability to land, community, Elders, and ancestors
item.description:
[预印本] Open Collections
This thesis explores the possibility of creating Indigenous-led sovereign virtual spaces. Thinking critically about the inherent tension between Indigenous people–whose struggle is primarily land-based–and the disembodied experience of virtual spaces, my research explores how we as Indigenous people might be guided by Indigenous philosophies of reciprocity and relationality to build frameworks of accountability to land, community, Elders, and ancestors that lead our development of sovereign virtual spaces. My methodology draws on research-creation and autopedagogy to guide the documentation of three Indigenous new media projects I developed over the course of my degree: Sage Plains, Last Words, and Sickle & Sash. Through Sage Plains, an RPG video game dealing with themes of Métis displacement, I explore accountability through visiting, particularly as it relates to my expansion of the game through a process of visiting with an Elder, and later integrating Métis Cree words and phrases into the gameplay. Through Last Words, a virtual art piece applying the concept of imagining otherwise to working with historical archives, as well as the exploration and interrogation of creative, ethical uses of artificial intelligence, I explore accountability to ancestors and land. Through Sickle & Sash, a podcast centered on Métis political discussion in opposition to cultural imperialism, I explore accountability to the sovereignty of my featured guests. All three projects explore unique points of engagement with Indigenous new media, as well as unique points of tension. By documenting, reflecting on, and analyzing my successes and failures in exercising accountability throughout the creation and development of these three projects, I affirm the outlined accountability structures as an essential framework for the creation of sovereign virtual spaces, and argue that these processes are essential aspects of modern-day decolonial praxis. Going further, I provide additional nuance on the application of these accountability structures as they pertain to the ethical boundaries that must be considered when translating traditional understandings of reciprocity and relationality to the realm of virtual spaces.

item.title: Creative ageing in a digital world: A protocol for a synthesis of arts-based innovations for culturally diverse older adults in Canada
item.description:
PLoS ONE
The forthcoming scoping review will synthesize evidence on arts-based and digital engagement initiatives that support social inclusion, mental health, and cultural expression among older adults, with a particular focus on structurally-disadvantaged populations. Rapid digital transformation in the arts, including virtual and augmented reality, digital storytelling, and generative artificial intelligence, has expanded opportunities for participation and creative expression. However, access remains uneven, and there is limited consolidated evidence on effectiveness, equity considerations, and best practices for implementation across diverse contexts. Guided by Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards, the forthcoming review will systematically search peer-reviewed and grey literature across major health, social science, and interdisciplinary databases from inception to October 2026. An integrated knowledge translation approach will be embedded throughout the review, engaging older adults, caregivers, community arts practitioners, and cultural leaders as active partners in refining search strategies, interpreting findings, and shaping dissemination. Data will be extracted and synthesized using both quantitative mapping and qualitative content analysis to identify program models, theoretical frameworks, implementation strategies, outcomes, and equity considerations. Findings will generate a comprehensive evidence map of effective and emerging practices, highlight barriers such as digital exclusion and cultural underrepresentation, and identify ethical and legal considerations in digital arts engagement. The review will inform the development of culturally safe, accessible, and inclusive arts and digital programming, and will provide actionable guidance for researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and community organizations seeking to enhance well-being, social connection, and cultural continuity among older adults.

item.title: Towards theorising the normative agency of Central Europe: iterative identities and norms shaping from a Global East perspective
item.description:
Pluriversal International Relations
This article examines under what conditions actors operating through a semi-peripheral regional format can develop an emergent form of normative agency. It treats the Three Seas Initiative as an illustrative Central European case, viewed through the Global East as a relational and epistemic positionality rather than a fixed geography. The article introduces the constructivist model of iterative identities and norms shaping, a heuristic framework tracing how previously articulated norms, identity narratives and regional role claims re-enter later political and institutional contexts and are reinterpreted, contested, amplified or institutionalised. The model identifies identity alignment and norm localisation as the principal conditions of regional normative agency, distinguishing conditional norm co-creation from compliance, locally bounded autonomy and failed agency. Empirically, the article analyses Three Seas Initiative summit declarations from 2016 to 2025, supplemented by institutional documents and selected European Union and North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) materials examining external recognition and convergence. The analysis reconstructs three phases of the initiative’s development: initial identity formation and the search for recognition; institutionalisation and the localisation of connectivity norms; and the post-2021 reinterpretation of infrastructure through resilience, security and eastern-flank vulnerability. The findings suggest that the initiative has generated limited and conditional normative agency through the regionally grounded reinterpretation of broader Euro-Atlantic normative templates. The case does not demonstrate autonomous norm creation but shows how historically norm-receiving actors may contribute to norm transformation when regional institutionalisation combines with wider recognition.

item.title: Evaluation of undergraduate medical students’ experiences, perceptions and learning from a deaf insights and British Sign Language course: a qualitative study
item.description:
BMC Medical Education
Abstract Background Deaf people experience healthcare inequities driven in part by limited deaf insights and specialist communication skills training in medical education. Evidence suggests deaf insights training and exposure to deaf culture and communication styles can improve students’ communication skills and understanding of deaf culture, yet it remains uncommon in undergraduate curricula. Methods We co-developed a Deaf Insights and British Sign Language student-selected component (SSC) for Year 3 medical students at Imperial College London with a deaf awareness trainer, and deaf insights advocate, who is also a deaf doctor, who shared their expertise and lived experiences of deaf culture, healthcare and patient journeys. The SSC comprised three weekly sessions (three hours each) focusing on health equity, communication, and reflective practice. We evaluated the SSC using an interpretivist qualitative approach with a dyadic interview and online survey. Data was analysed thematically using transformative learning theory as a sensitising lens. Results Across three cohorts in 2025-2026, forty students completed the SSC. Students described learning from the SSC that appeared to be aligned with the initial steps of transformative learning theory. Students discussed their assumptions being challenged and perspectives changing. This included a new understanding of deaf culture alongside a recognition of healthcare barriers and inequities faced by deaf people, and a perceived increase in their confidence in communicating with deaf people. This learning appears to have been facilitated by the co-design, co-delivery and opportunity to interact directly with deaf trainers and advocates. Students reflected upon their learning during group discussions and described intentions to act upon these new insights by changing their own practice and educating others regarding their new learning, hoping to act as advocates for deaf people in future. Conclusion Co-creation and co-delivery of an SSC in deaf insights training with deaf trainers and advocates shows features consistent with the initial stages of transformative learning occurring in undergraduate medical students. Our approach and findings may be of interest to other institutions developing similar training. Wider adoption of this model could help improve students’ confidence and understanding of how to meet the needs of deaf people which may in turn contribute to improving health equity for deaf individuals.

item.title: Effects of paradoxical mindset on tourists’ eWOM and revisit intentions
item.description:
Journal Of Vacation Marketing
Drawing on the value–attitude–behavior (VAB) model, the current study aims to identify the determinants that inspire customers’ electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) and revisit intention in unmanned smart hotels in addition to the moderating influence of perceived risks. Furthermore, a multigroup analysis was conducted to investigate the differences between business and leisure tourists. This study adopts a quantitative approach where data is gathered from 396 unmanned smart hotel customers from China. Structural equation modeling was employed to test the proposed relationships. The results indicate that experience co-creation, memorable smart hotel experience, hedonic value, and utilitarian value significantly and positively influence the eWOM and revisit intention of unmanned smart hotels. For moderating relationship, privacy risk serves as a full moderator in the relationship between hedonic value, utilitarian value and attitude as well as eWOM and revisit intention. However, performance risk is found to be a partial moderator since it only moderates between perceived values and attitude but not between perceived values and related behavioral intentions. Meanwhile, results reveal the differences in moderating effects between business and leisure travelers. These findings provide important insights into whether, how, and for whom perceived values yield positive marketing outcomes, and offer practical guidance for smart hotel managers and smart devices manufacturers on how to provide better experiences for their customers.

item.title: EXPRESS: Participation Governance in Consumer and AI Co-creation: Whether to Intervene and How to Design It
item.description:
Production and Operations Management
Artificial intelligence reshapes digital mass customization by altering the structure of consumer co-creation. When consumers start from a draft generated by artificial intelligence rather than a blank canvas, outcomes are jointly determined by two stages: whether consumers initiate co-creation and, conditional on participation, how much refinement effort they exert. This separation makes participation a governable design margin—an issue that is largely muted in traditional blank-canvas customization, where participation and effort are tightly bundled. Partnering with a leading United States online retailer of personalized photo products, we study whether and how firm interventions at the participation stage shape downstream purchase outcomes. We develop a two-stage model in which, relative to a baseline with organic participation, a nudge lowers start-up frictions and expands voluntary entry, whereas a mandate serves as a strong boundary-case intervention that guarantees entry but can weaken how participation translates into purchase, generating a reach–efficiency trade-off. We examine these predictions in two randomized experiments. In Study 1, a light-touch nudge increases participation by 5.98 percentage points and raises revenue and order frequency. The evidence is consistent with gains arising primarily through expanded entry into consumer co-creation with artificial intelligence. In Study 2, mandates increase participation relative to nudges, but we find no clear evidence of additional gains in purchase or revisit intentions. Instead, mandates increase low-value participation, in which consumers exert minimal effort and report low purchase intention. Together, these findings show that in mass customization enabled by artificial intelligence, participation governance is a consequential design choice: firms must consider not only how many consumers initiate co-creation, but also whether the participation they induce creates downstream value.

item.title: "Catching lightning in a bottle": How Blind or Low Vision Creators Navigate Ideation Across Creative Domains
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Ideation, i.e., generating, capturing, organizing, and evaluating ideas, is foundational to creative practices; yet little is known about how blind and low vision (BLV) creators engage in ideation. We conducted interviews with 20 BLV creators working in different domains including poetry, music production, tactile graphics, digital drawing, and mixed-media arts. Our findings reveal how participants established accessible creative workflows under social and institutional constraints, drew inspiration from diverse physical and digital sources, captured and organized ideas across text, audio, visual, and physical modalities, and evaluated their work through human and AI feedback. We discuss how ableist norms and accessibility breakdowns cascade across ideation pathways, progressively narrowing BLV individuals’ creative possibilities. Finally, we offer design considerations for building accessible ideation support tools that amplify BLV creators’ distinctive practices.

item.title: Synthesizing and Evaluating a Visual Feedback Framework for Accessible Content Creation
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Many blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals are interested in visual content creation, yet creative tools provide limited feedback for visual outputs during authoring. We synthesized and evaluated a visual feedback framework for creative tasks—we first conducted a purpose-specific literature review of 54 accessibility papers on BLV creators’ feedback needs and then refined the resulting framework through expert review interviews with nine BLV creators. We identify key feedback components for creative work, including object and people information, spatial layout, intent-based checking and suggestions, version differences, and visual aesthetics. We also outline delivery guidelines emphasizing hierarchical control, multimodal interaction, real-time verification, non-visual language, and transparency about AI accuracy. Our findings show that creative authoring requires more detailed and intent-driven feedback than passive consumption, particularly to support iterative decision-making and diverse creative goals. Rather than a prescriptive checklist, this framework offers a practical foundation for researchers and practitioners when designing and evaluating accessible creative tools.

item.title: A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit: unraveling the evolving role of customers’ emotional intelligence and perspective taking in promoting value co-creation behavior
item.description:
SAM Advanced Management Journal
Purpose This study aims to develop a conceptual model which aims to test the contribution of emotional intelligence in strengthening value co-creation behavior, with perspective taking included as a mediator. Design/methodology/approach The model was tested using cross-sectional data, which were collected from a sample of 338 customers selected using a convenience sampling technique in selected restaurants within the restaurant industry in Dodoma region. Findings The analyses using covariance-based structural equation modeling indicate that all hypotheses were supported, suggesting that emotional intelligence drives customers toward demonstrating value co-creation behavior through perspective taking. Practical implications Thus, service organizations should encourage customers to demonstrate positive emotions during the service encounters as strategic resources to ensure effective participation in value co-creation. Originality/value This study is one of among the few studies that have recently examined competencies of customers as a driver of value co-creation behavior. The study advances insights and fuel debates regarding the equal importance of considering both the competence of frontline employees and customers as co-actors in value co-creation.

item.title: Designing phygital tourism experiencescapes for tourist well-being: a transformative service framework
item.description:
Journal of Services Marketing
Purpose This paper aims to develop a Transformative Service Research (TSR)-informed framework explaining how phygital tourism experiencescapes can be designed to foster tourist well-being. It addresses limited understanding of how hybrid physical–digital service environments can operate as well-being-oriented transformative systems beyond technological enhancement and engagement. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts an integrative conceptual approach because phygital transformative tourism experiencescapes constitute an emergent, multidisciplinary and theoretically fragmented domain. It synthesizes customer experience, tourist well-being and service research through thematic clustering to clarify relationships among service environments, tourists’ interpretive processes and well-being-oriented transformation. This synthesis generates six framework elements: experiencescape stimuli, decoding mechanisms, experience types, transformative mechanisms, well-being outcomes and experiential marketing as a design layer. Findings The paper proposes a Stimulus–Experience–Well-being framework. Phygital experiencescape stimuli are interpreted through sensoriality, cognition, affectivity, sociability, conativity, pragmatism and lifestyle alignment mechanisms, producing experience types such as immersion, refreshment, reflection, volunteering, challenge, education, entertainment, socialization and sensory experience. These experiences activate transformative mechanisms that shape hedonic, eudaimonic, collective and occupational well-being, while poorly configured technologies may generate overload, technostress or negative transformation. Practical implications The framework guides managers to align experiential marketing practices – multisensory design, customization, co-creation, gamification and theming – with intended experience pathways, well-being outcomes and phygital tools. Social implications The study highlights how phygital tourism can support participation, cultural awareness, empathy and responsible behavior. Originality/value The study extends TSR into phygital tourism, refines stimulus–organism–response logic by specifying two mediating layers, and integrates experiential marketing as a service-system design lever for transforming hybrid experiences into well-being outcomes.

item.title: Phygital customer experience and the adoption of immersive technologies in hospitality: an exploratory study with a value co-creation perspective
item.description:
Journal of Services Marketing
Purpose This study aims to explore immersive-technology adoption in hospitality through the Phygital Customer Experience (PH-CX) framework. PH-CX extends existing technology acceptance, service-dominant logic, omnichannel and customer-journey perspectives by emphasizing embodied, co-created and human-centered experience across physical, digital and artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated interactions. Design/methodology/approach Using Bayesian Networks, the study examines probabilistic dependencies among perceived usefulness, collaborative value, responsive co-creation attitudes and intention to use immersive technologies. Data was collected from 208 participants exposed to an AI-supported immersive hotel journey scenario. The analysis is exploratory and identifies conditional associations rather than causal effects or latent-variable relationships. Findings Adoption intention was conditionally associated with perceived usefulness, collaborative value and responsiveness to service innovation. The findings suggest that immersive-hospitality engagement involves functional, relational and participatory conditions beyond usefulness alone. However, the item-level results are hypothesis-generating and do not demonstrate PH-CX’s incremental predictive superiority over technology acceptance model (TAM) or service-dominant logic. Research limitations/implications The scenario-based, cross-sectional bayesian network (BN) design cannot model latent constructs, measurement error, mediation or causal effects. Future studies should validate PH-CX dimensions and compare TAM, TAM-plus-service-dominant logic (SDL) and PH-CX models using structural equation modeling, longitudinal designs and holdout-sample prediction. Practical implications Hotels can implement PH-CX through phased AI concierge pilots, cross-platform data integration and guest co-creation mechanisms. Relevant metrics include booking conversion, AI resolution rates, cross-channel engagement, co-creation participation and net promoter score (NPS). Ethical implementation requires transparency, opt-in participation, privacy safeguards, accessibility and human escalation options. Social implications Human-centered phygital hospitality requires safeguards against digital exclusion, surveillance and loss of human warmth. Transparency, agency, equity, privacy and non-digital alternatives are essential for inclusive and trustworthy service innovation. Originality/value The study advances PH-CX as a theory-extending framework linking usefulness, co-creation, embodied experience and ethical safeguards in immersive hospitality. It also proposes experience-design orientation as a future research profile and offers a phased implementation framework for responsible phygital service design.

item.title: CSR communication on social media: the impact of message source and co-creation cues on credibility, engagement, and e-WOM
item.description:
Journal of Communication Management
Purpose Amid stakeholder skepticism and organizations' reliance on static, informational posts, this study aims to assess which configurations of message source (corporate vs. non-governmental organization (NGO)) and co-creation cues (high vs. low) stimulate source credibility, consumer engagement, and electronic word of mouth (e-WOM) in corporate social responsibility communication (CSR-C) on social media (SM), grounded in stakeholder theory. Design/methodology/approach A 2 × 2 between-subjects factorial experiment was conducted with 406 active Facebook users in India. Data were analyzed using two-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and partial least squares structural equation modeling multigroup analysis. Findings High co-creation cues significantly increased source credibility, consumer engagement, and e-WOM, diminishing the independent effect of message source. NGO-attributed posts produced higher e-WOM than corporate posts, but only under high co-creation. Consumer engagement partially mediated the effect of source credibility on e-WOM. Practical implications Practitioners should prioritize participatory message design (high co-creation cues) over source attribution, and treat NGO partnerships as effective for e-WOM only when posts invite participation. Originality/value This is among the first studies to assess which message source and co-creation cues jointly shape CSR-C outcomes on SM. It shows that co-creation cues, not source identity, are the primary driver, identifies consumer engagement as the mechanism linking credibility to e-WOM, and locates these effects in the under-examined Indian mandated-CSR context.

item.title: Negotiating professional identity in the creative industries: the REC framework for Human–AI creative work
item.description:
Career Development International
Purpose This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes professional identity in the creative industries. Although prior research has largely emphasized the technological capabilities and industry-level implications of AI, limited attention has been devoted to how creative professionals themselves interpret and negotiate its consequences for creativity, authorship, and career development. Design/methodology/approach An inductive qualitative design is conducted based on 40 semi-structured interviews with professionals from the Italian audiovisual industry, including actors, directors, screenwriters, technicians, and AI experts. Data were analyzed using the Gioia methodology. Findings Findings show that AI does not simply support creative work but disrupts established understandings of what it means to be a creative professional. Three interconnected forms of identity work emerge: resisting, extending, and crafting (REC). While some participants defend the human and symbolic foundations of creativity, others embrace AI as a source of experimentation and new skill formation. More critically, AI also generates identity ambiguity and fragmentation, blurring boundaries between human originality, technological assistance, and professional legitimacy. Originality/value This work addresses an important gap in AI and creative work research by shifting attention from technological adoption to the identity-level consequences of AI. Through a unique and heterogeneous dataset spanning multiple creative occupations, the study introduces the REC framework and conceptualizes AI as a disruptive identity force that simultaneously enables, threatens, and redefines career sustainability.

item.title: Dynamics of collective creativity in AI art competitions
item.description:
PNAS Nexus
Abstract Creativity is a fundamental part of cultural evolution, but the mechanisms by which groups produce novelty are notoriously difficult to infer from the historical record. Iterated learning experiments have shown that cultural transmission reliably distorts artifacts toward the inductive biases of learners, but most of this work uses linear chains of human participants, and it is unclear how these dynamics play out in the networked, human-AI systems that increasingly shape cultural production. In this study, we analyze one such system: Artbreeder, which hosts daily “remix parties” in which users iteratively build on each other's work from a single seed image, producing branching lineages of images co-created by humans and generative AI. Using 130,882 images from 368 remix parties over 13 months, we find that images become less novel over the course of a party and that each remix step moves less far from its parents, consistent with the stabilization seen in iterated learning experiments, and that late-stage images drift toward the platform's dominant portrait style. More novel “parent” images produce more novel and more complex “children.” More novel children attract more likes but are not remixed more, whereas more complex children are remixed less. Finally, larger remix parties produce images that are more novel but less complex.

item.title: Transformative learning in farmer research networks: insights from Eastern and Southern Africa
item.description:
International Journal of Agricultural Sustainability
Farmer research networks are collaborative platforms where farmers, researchers, extension workers, and NGOs co-create knowledge, experiment with innovations, and tackle local challenges through joint learning and action. Although interest in these networks is growing, there remains a limited understanding of how learning occurs within them. This study draws on qualitative data from nine networks active between 2015 and 2024 in Kenya, Malawi and Uganda. It reveals that these networks foster individual and collective transformation. The process is dynamic, multi-dimensional, technical, relational, and emotional, shaped by diverse knowledge systems and social interactions. Emotional engagement , enhanced motivation, deepened reflection, and prompted identity shifts. Networks function not only as sites of knowledge co-creation and learning but also as cultural and emotional spaces where agricultural visions and identities are negotiated and reshaped. Farmers assumed roles as researchers and educators, adapting agroecological innovations and experimenting with solutions to ecological and livelihood challenges. The key enabling factors were trust among members, inclusive facilitation, institutional memory, and strong local leadership. Progress was constrained by entrenched gender norms, hierarchical extension practices, and rigid social structures. Sustaining transformative learning calls for continued investment in facilitation capacity, inclusive leadership and institutional structures that embed networks within broader innovation systems.

item.title: Design literacy as an mediator: An empirical study on AIGC-assisted intangible cultural heritage design
item.description:
The Design Journal
Although AI-generated content (AIGC) is increasingly integrated into cultural heritage design, few empirical studies have examined how users’ design literacy and educational backgrounds shape their engagement with AIGC in culturally embedded design tasks. This paper uses mixed methods to investigate AIGC in Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) design, using Quanzhou Festival Lanterns as a case study. A 17-week teaching experiment involving 105 undergraduates was conducted to develop a structured evaluation framework for AIGC-assisted ICH design. The findings indicate that AIGC significantly enhances creative expression, particularly when supported by strong design literacy. Comparative analysis demonstrates that design literacy may play a significant explanatory role in the process of AIGC-assisted culture creativity: design majors tend to use AIGC for cultural semantic organization and design iteration, whereas non-design majors focus more on the novelty of visual forms, resulting in works that are relatively limited in terms of the depth of cultural expression.

item.title: Organizing Creative Labor in the Age of AI: Institutional Differences and Transnational Connections Across the US and EU
item.description:
The Journal of Arts Management Law and Society
This paper examines how cultural and creative workers (CCW) in the United States and European Union have organized in response to the rise of artificial intelligence in cultural and creative industries since 2023. Drawing on documentary analysis and interviews that contextualize and interpret the secondary material, it examines parallel developments in the two contexts to explore how different institutional settings shape CCWs’ collective responses to AI. The analysis highlights distinct institutional pathways and mobilization repertoires, yet increasingly shared concerns around authorship, consent, transparency, and remuneration, pointing toward increasingly interconnected CCW ecosystems across geographical boundaries. The paper thus argues that AI-related mobilization is shaped both by institutional contexts and emerging transnational connections, contributing to broader debates on creative labor, collective organization, and the governance of emerging technologies.

item.title: A fashion specific framework for artificial intelligence literacy in higher education
item.description:
Discover Artificial Intelligence
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming every dimension of the fashion industry—from creative ideation and pattern generation to supply chain optimization, trend forecasting, and personalized retail. Yet the higher education institutions charged with preparing tomorrow’s fashion professionals remain structurally, pedagogically, and conceptually unprepared for this transformation. This paper argues that the challenge is not simply one of adding AI tools to existing curricula; it is, more fundamentally, a question of literacy. Drawing on a critical integrative review of interdisciplinary scholarship across AI education, digital literacy theory, fashion pedagogy, and industry workforce analysis, this paper examines three interlocking questions: What is AI literacy, and how has its conceptualization evolved? What theoretical and conceptual frameworks currently govern AI literacy discourse, and how might they be adapted for the creative disciplines? And, critically, do fashion higher education students require a form of AI literacy that is fashion-specific—and if so, what form should it take? The paper proposes a novel conceptual framework, the Fashion AI Literacy Framework ( FALF ) and outlines concrete curricular pathways for implementation. The framework is presented as a conceptual proposition that requires empirical validation. The argument advanced here is both urgent and structural: generic AI literacy, however well-designed, may not fully equip fashion students to navigate the creative, ethical, commercial, and cultural terrain that defines their discipline. On the evidence reviewed here, a domain-specific approach is better understood as needed rather than optional.

item.title: The rebirth of the author: writing critical social theory in the time of generative AI
item.description:
Theory and Society
Abstract Sociologists face the pressing question of how large language model-based technologies can contribute to social theorising. Several social scientists have called for a greater integration of generative AI tools in the social sciences and humanities to speed and scale up the production of social theory. In this article, we adopt a more cautious approach, reflecting on how the adoption of generative AI raises foundational questions about the construction, refinement and evaluation of critical social theory. To make this argument, we create and critically analyse a speculative piece of dystopian sociological fiction. This enables us to explore the values and practices of critical social theory authorship. We argue that authorship must be ‘recentred’, particularly with regard to four key values of authorial practice: (1) standpoint, (2) creativity, (3) pluralism and (4) accountability. In the present moment, the use of generative AI as substitution for authorial practices redefines and potentially threatens authorship in ways that problematises its particular use in generating critical social theory. With regards to standpoint, generative AI technologies run the risk of reproducing an ‘abstract masculinity’ that feminist scholars have long written against. The relational wonder at the heart of social theory creativity is undermined by generative AI use, as is the pluralism of creativity. Generative AI also flattens and overlooks pluralism of voice, as well as dilutes authorial accountability. We sociologists need to defend and rearticulate what we contribute to social theory and its concomitant politics, both in the theories themselves and in the project of social theorising. It is with this in mind that we call for the ‘rebirth’ - that is, the recentralisation - of the human author in critical social theory creation.

item.title: Explainable AI in Neural Poetry Generation: Beyond Attention
item.description:
Applied AI Letters
ABSTRACT Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is increasingly important for ensuring transparency and trust in neural systems; however, its applicability to creative text generation remains limited. Neural poetry generation models produce linguistically coherent and stylistically rich outputs, yet explaining decisions such as metaphor construction, emotional tone, and thematic development remains unresolved. This systematic literature review synthesizes 26 peer‐reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a predefined protocol across four major digital libraries. The analysis identifies a fundamental mismatch between existing XAI paradigms and the properties of generative modeling. We propose a taxonomy distinguishing classification‐native methods from generation‐compatible approaches, highlighting their differing assumptions. Based on established criteria of contrastivity, selectivity, and faithfulness, we show that attention mechanisms lack causal validity as explanatory tools. To consolidate these findings, we introduce a unified failure framework comprising five interacting structural limitations: token–semantic mismatch, attention non‐causality, classification–generation incompatibility, evaluation collapse, and human–model ontological misalignment. These limitations collectively constrain the effectiveness of current XAI methods in creative contexts. Our findings indicate that advancing explainability in neural poetry generation requires a shift toward semantic‐level representations, causal intervention‐based approaches, and human‐centered evaluation frameworks that incorporate aesthetic and interpretive dimensions.

item.title: DEEPFAKES AND CRIMINAL LIABILITY IN NIGERIA: EMERGING CHALLENGES FOR THE CRIMINAL JUSTICE SYSTEM
item.description:
Journal of Jurisprudence, International Law and Contemporary Legal Issues
Deepfake technology has transformed the production and circulation of audio-visual material by enabling artificial intelligence systems to create highly realistic synthetic representations of persons, voices, events and statements. Although the technology has legitimate applications in entertainment, education, accessibility and creative production, its malicious deployment presents serious challenges for criminal law and the administration of criminal justice. Deepfakes can facilitate impersonation, fraud, extortion, identity theft, non-consensual sexual imagery, reputational attacks, election manipulation, cyberbullying and the fabrication or alteration of digital evidence. Nigeria presently has no specific legal framework on deepfake creation or distribution. Nevertheless, conduct involving malicious deepfakes may fall within existing offences under the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015 (as amended in 2024), the Criminal Code Act, the Penal Code, the Administration of Criminal Justice Act 2015, the Evidence Act 2011 (as amended in 2023), the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and other relevant laws. This article examined the extent to which those provisions can respond to deepfake-enabled criminality. It suggested that the present framework is fragmented and often dependent upon the purpose, manner and consequences of the deepfake rather than the synthetic manipulation itself. The article also examined attribution, mens rea, jurisdiction, authentication, evidential reliability and the difficulties created by anonymous and cross-border perpetrators. Drawing from comparative approaches in the United Kingdom and Kenya, the article proposed a Nigerian Deepfake and Synthetic Media framework as well as institutional checks, while ensuring safeguards for journalism, sattire, research and artistic expressions.

item.title: USING GENERATIVE AI TO CREATE LANGUAGE GAMES IN THE ENGLISH CLASSROOM
item.description:
Центральноазиатский журнал образования и инноваций
The paper examines how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT can be used to create language games for English lessons. It describes the main types of AI-generated games (interactive stories, vocabulary riddles, quizzes and role-plays), shows how they are produced with simple prompts, and discusses their effect on learner motivation and teacher workload. Generative AI is presented not as a replacement for the teacher but as a creative assistant that makes gamified lessons quick to prepare and easy to personalise.

item.title: Integration of artificial intelligence in quality improvement projects for undergraduate nursing students: Enhancing nursing education through innovative applications
item.description:
Journal of Nursing Education and Practice
Background and objective: Nursing faculty have been hesitant to incorporate artificial intelligence into coursework due to various reasons, including the risk of affecting academic integrity and the potential for receiving inaccurate information. As nursing cohorts continue to grow, innovative approaches are needed to meet learning objectives; such as artificial intelligence. Incorporating artificial intelligence into group projects may increase responsible, ethical, and critical use of artificial intelligence and support programs in managing larger cohorts. The purpose of this initiative was to integrate artificial intelligence into the literature review process for a quality improvement group project to develop students’ ability to use artificial intelligence responsibly, ethically, and critically. This approach included validating the accuracy of artificial intelligence generated information. Methods: This initiative was offered as an honors conversion opportunity within the Clinical Science II course to undergraduate nursing students. Six students opted to participate and were divided into two groups of three. Groups selected a topic related to the course content and aligned it with one of the Joint Commission national patient safety goals. Groups developed a clinical question, search strategy, conducted a literature review, and used artificial intelligence to identify evidence. Results: Benefits of using artificial intelligence included the generation of creative ideas, provision of workflow steps, and a broad range of solutions. Challenges included a lack of concrete examples and a tendency for artificial intelligence generated information to be more practical than theoretical. Groups found artificial intelligence generated findings aligned with most articles from their literature reviews. Conclusions: Incorporating the utilization of artificial intelligence into nursing curriculums can help programs monitor usage while managing growing cohorts. Allowing students to engage with artificial intelligence under guided instruction enhances understanding of its practical applications in clinical settings. This will better prepare students for real-world practice while ensuring academic integrity is maintained.

item.title: Generative AI and Copyrightability in the United States: Human Authorship, Creative Control, and AI-Assisted Works
item.description:
International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
The U.S. Copyright Office has released its report Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability. This paper explores the copyrightability of AI-generated and AI-assisted works in the United States, focusing on that report and on the jurisprudence of human authorship. It examines the constitutional and statutory bases of human authorship, the importance of Burrow-Giles, Feist, Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid and Thaler v. Perlmutter, and how the Copyright Office has dealt with prompting, human-authored inputs, selection, arrangement, modification and the assistive use of AI. The paper shows that the United States has adopted a case-by-case approach: the use of AI as a tool does not defeat protection, but copyright extends only to expression created by a human author and not to material generated by AI itself. Under current technology, prompts alone do not generally provide sufficient control, but human expression that is perceptible in the output, creative selection and arrangement, and meaningful modification can be protected. The paper sets out the strengths and weaknesses of this approach and suggests more explicit registration, evidentiary and guidance practices, while maintaining the human-authorship requirement.

item.title: RANANO-Recreating Nano Banana Using Diffusion Model
item.description:
Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology
RANANO is an integrated artificial intelligence-based multimedia creation platform developed to combine multiple creative functionalities within a single web-based interface. The system addresses the fragmented workflow involved in using separate applications for image generation, image enhancement, video creation, animated text generation, and user guidance. RANANO uses a trained diffusion model for text-to-image generation, where the trained model checkpoint is integrated into the application for inference. The platform also incorporates image enhancement using super-resolution, video generation from selected images, animated text generation, and a voice assistant for interactive guidance. The system follows a modular architecture in which the frontend communicates with backend services responsible for model inference, image processing, multimedia generation, and output management. The diffusion model is trained using a prepared dataset, while the trained checkpoint is subsequently loaded during application execution without repeated training. Functional testing was conducted across the major modules, including checkpoint loading, prompt processing, image generation, image enhancement, video generation, animated text, voice interaction, output display and storage, and frontend-backend integration. All twelve test cases documented in the project were successfully passed. The results demonstrate that RANANO provides a unified and modular approach for AI-assisted multimedia creation while reducing the need to switch between multiple tools. The system also provides scope for future improvements in computational efficiency, processing time, and multimedia generation capabilities.

item.title: SUSTAINOPRENEURSHIP: A THEORY OF ENTREPRENEURIAL APPROACH WITH SUSTAINABILITY
item.description:
Journal of Social Sciences Development
Sustainopreneurship is a theoretical approach that is a combination of entrepreneurial orientation and sustainability requirements to solve the complex socio-environmental problems. This paper proposes a theory of sustainopreneurship as a process of seeking opportunities in which entrepreneurs create innovative, scalable and economically viable solutions that not only create social equity but also regenerate the environment and create economic value in the long-term. Sustainopreneurship is based on the idea of a balanced triple-bottom-line logic, which is embedded into the opportunity recognition, the orchestration of the resources and the creation of value processes, unlike the traditional entrepreneurship, which is generally driven by a logic of profit, or the social entrepreneurship, which is generally driven by a logic of social impact. The theory is based on a synthesis of the fields of entrepreneurship, sustainability science, and strategic management and highlights six constructs: sustainability-oriented opportunity recognition, creation of triple-bottom-line value, orchestration of regenerative resources, stakeholder co-creation, impact scalability, and adaptive sustainability capability. The framework is comprised of a set of eight theoretical propositions: a vision of links between sustainability challenges and entrepreneurial outcomes within specific boundary conditions. Antecedents, core processes and long-term outcomes are also distinguished, to create an integrated conceptual model for the study. Sustainopreneurship contributes to the academic discourse by integrating the two literatures of entrepreneurship and sustainability, by adding a dimension of creating regenerative value as a key entrepreneurial process, and by introducing a dimension of process into the triple bottom line, as a goal, rather than only an outcome. It's a theoretical underpinning to guide practitioners, policymakers and educators on how to try to go about striking a balance between benefits and losses to the planet and its people, and profitability. Finally, Sustainopreneurship is seen as a paradigm for a resilient, inclusive and sustainable economic model amidst global uncertainties.

item.title: The “Breath” of Persuasion: Corporeality as the Missing Link between Classical Rhetoric and Discourse in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
Rhetoric and Communications
Abstract: The article examines the classical Aristotelian model of persuasion, based on the triad of ethos, pathos, and logos, but from a new and different perspective, namely, within the context of corporeality and embodied cognition (embodiment). According to this understanding, the mind, thought, and language do not exist independently of the body but are directly conditioned by our physical experience and senses. The hypothesis is that the deficit of artificial intelligence in comparison with the living orator is not merely moral or value-based – it is, above all, physical: generative models have no breath, weight, spontaneity, or presence here and now. This bodily absence underlies what classical rhetoric describes abstractly as the absence of ethos and pathos. The methodology is innovative and incorporates auto-cyberethnographic observation, as well as internal and external observation. The analysis is based on three stage experiments (Improbotics, Annie Dorsen, and Interrobang / Chatbot Challenge), in which the boundary between machine-generated and live performance is literally tested before an audience, complemented by the evocative power of the literary voice of Zdravka Evtimova. Three forms of art – literature, theatre, and oratory – are examined from a creative and a methodological perspective that has not been explored to date. The conclusions drawn from the analysis indicate that rhetorical education, which may form part of actors’ training during and beyond the third decade of the 21st century, at a time when artificial intelligence is developing and being increasingly utilized dynamically, requires a return to the body – to voice, breathing, and presence – as a primary rather than a secondary source of persuasiveness. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, rhetoric, corporeality, embodied cognition (embodiment), ethos, pathos, logos, performance, breath, presence.
